title: Logical relational schema
what: Tables and references at design level: keys, cardinalities and which table owns a fact — still no storage engine decisions.
why: Move from business nouns to a checkable structure: every relationship now has a home and a direction.
when: After the conceptual ER pass, before physical naming, indexing and platform choices.
read: Each box is a table; read keys first, then the reference arrows from foreign key to primary key.
Crow's-foot marks state how many children a parent may have — claims, not constraints enforced here.
inputs: The entity list from the conceptual model
pitfalls: Do not put a foreign key on both sides.
A many-to-many without a join table hides a missing entity.
limits: Logical only: datatypes, indexes and platform types are declared in the physical model, not here.

title: Physical representation and datatype documentation
what: SQL objects with their dependencies: which view reads which table, which table feeds which report.
why: Know the blast radius of a schema change before you make it.
when: Impact analysis before renaming, splitting or dropping database objects.
read: Arrows point from a definition to the objects that consume it.
A shared lookup table with many consumers is a deliberate coupling, not an accident.
pitfalls: Do not treat a missing arrow as proof of no dependency — dynamic SQL and applications are outside the model until declared.
Do not delete a consumer from the diagram to make a change look safe.
limits: Declared dependencies only; runtime introspection of a live database is out of scope.

title: Document and embedded-object schema
what: A document model: nested objects, arrays and embedded structures with their containment rules.
why: Tree-shaped data needs its own contract — tables of one row type do not describe nesting.
when: Designing JSON documents, message payloads, or any hierarchical record.
read: Containment reads top-down: each level owns the fields below it.
Arrays are plural by contract, not by current length.
pitfalls: Do not flatten a tree into parallel tables just because it feels relational.
An optional node with required children is usually a modeling mistake.
limits: Structural contract only; no validation engine runs against live documents.

title: Property-graph schema
what: Nodes and edges with properties: the schema of a property graph, including which labels and properties exist.
why: Graph stores still need contracts — "schemaless" without a written agreement becomes archaeology.
when: Designing or reviewing a property-graph model (nodes, edge types, properties).
read: Node labels are types; edge labels are typed relationships.
Properties attach to the node or edge that owns them.
pitfalls: Do not model every relationship as a generic "related" edge.
Do not store on an edge what belongs to the node.
limits: Declared schema only; no graph query execution.

title: Key-value structure and lookup contract
what: A key-value space: key shapes, value payloads, and the lookup contract between them.
why: Make key design a reviewed decision — it decides distribution, collisions and every access pattern.
when: Designing caches, key-value stores, or any lookup-first data structure.
read: Keys are the contract; values are opaque to readers of the key space.
Lookup paths start at the key, never the value.
pitfalls: Do not design keys you cannot construct from what the reader already knows.
Do not hide a second lookup path the contract does not mention.
limits: Contract documentation; no cache behaviour is simulated.

title: Wide-column and access-pattern design
what: A wide-column layout: rows keyed for the queries they must serve, column families grouped by access pattern.
why: In wide-column stores the query writes the schema — documenting which access pattern owns which family prevents expensive mistakes.
when: Designing or reviewing Cassandra/Bigtable-style tables.
read: Read from the partition key outward: what is looked up together lives together.
Column families are access patterns, not topics.
inputs: The queries the system must answer
pitfalls: Do not model wide-column tables relationally and expect the queries to work.
Do not create a family nobody reads.
limits: Design documentation; no distribution or compaction behaviour is modeled.

title: Semantic domains and candidate bindings
what: Semantic domains: named value sets with their rules, and which fields bind to which domain.
why: Shared meaning beats shared spelling — a domain contract stops "status" meaning six different things.
when: Whenever the same concept appears in several tables, payloads or teams.
read: Domains are named rule sets; fields borrow them.
A field bound to two conflicting domains is a defect, not a convenience.
inputs: The value sets and their rules
pitfalls: Do not clone a domain instead of referencing it.
Do not bind by name when a reference exists.
limits: Declared bindings only; the registry validates references, not your data at rest.

title: Catalog, database and schema organization
what: Namespace hierarchy: catalogs, databases and schemas, and where each object lives in it.
why: Ownership and environment boundaries live in namespaces; getting them on paper prevents "it worked in dev".
when: Organizing many objects across environments, teams or catalogs.
read: Nesting is ownership: an object has exactly one home.
Cross-namespace references are explicit, annotated contracts.
pitfalls: Do not let objects drift between namespaces without a migration note.
Do not hide cross-namespace dependencies in names.
limits: Organizational documentation; no deployment is performed from this view.

title: Hybrid local/cloud deployment
what: A deployment split across on-premises and cloud environments: what runs where, and the links between them.
why: Hybrid designs fail at the seams; the seam list is the point of the diagram.
when: Planning or reviewing any system spanning local and cloud infrastructure.
read: Environment boundaries are the thick lines — everything crossing them is an explicit link.
Data gravity arrows point where state lives, not where compute happens.
inputs: The cross-boundary links and their protocols
pitfalls: Do not leave the boundary link unnamed — it is usually the riskiest part.
Do not duplicate a component in both environments without saying which is authoritative.
limits: Structural documentation; no latency, failover or cost model is implied.

title: Data-flow diagram (Yourdon/Gane–Sarson idiom)
what: Processes, data stores and external entities with the flows between them: where data moves, not who decides.
why: DFDs expose missing flows and orphan stores that a task diagram never shows.
when: Mapping information movement through a system before deciding on implementation.
read: Every arrow is data in motion, labeled with what it carries.
Stores are data at rest; a store nobody reads is a question, not a fact.
pitfalls: Do not draw control flow — arrows carry data, not instructions.
Do not let a process have inputs but no outputs.
limits: Flow documentation; no simulation of the data actually moving.

title: Event distribution / streaming integration
what: Producers, topics and consumers of an event stream: who publishes what, who subscribes, and the contracts between them.
why: Streaming systems fail on contracts, not on brokers; the diagram is where the contract gets reviewed.
when: Designing or auditing event-driven integration.
read: Topics are the joints: everything else attaches to them.
Consumers read at their own pace — the diagram shows subscriptions, not delivery guarantees.
pitfalls: Do not draw point-to-point links around the broker — it hides the coupling the topics create.
Do not leave the schema owner off a topic.
limits: Integration documentation; no throughput, ordering or replay semantics are modeled.

title: Dataset lineage and derivation
what: Where each dataset comes from: sources, transformations and the datasets they produce, end to end.
why: Every number on a report should answer "from where" in one look.
when: Auditing data products, debugging a wrong number, or onboarding to a pipeline.
read: Read right-to-left from the report: each arrow is a derivation step you can inspect.
A dataset with no recorded source is an assumption, not a fact.
pitfalls: Do not skip the boring intermediate datasets — they are where errors hide.
Do not draw lineage at a granularity you cannot actually inspect.
limits: Declared lineage; no data actually flows when you read this.

title: Valid-time and recorded-time model
what: Bitemporal data: when a fact was true (valid time) versus when we learned it (record time), modeled explicitly.
why: Most "history" tables answer only one of those questions; the diagram keeps both honest.
when: Designing audit trails, corrections, or any as-of reporting.
read: Each fact carries two clocks; reads pick a point on each.
A correction adds a row — it never edits the past in place.
pitfalls: Do not overwrite a fact when you mean to correct it.
Do not confuse "when it happened" with "when it was entered".
limits: Model documentation; no temporal query evaluation.

title: Dimensional warehouse / star schema
what: A star schema: one fact table surrounded by dimensions, with grain declared.
why: The star makes analytical queries legible — and the grain declaration prevents the classic double-count.
when: Designing marts, cubes or any reporting model.
read: The fact table is events or measurements; dimensions answer who/what/where/when.
Every fact row means exactly one thing — that is the grain.
pitfalls: Do not mix grains in one fact table.
Do not let a dimension quietly become a second fact table.
limits: Model documentation; no aggregation is computed by this view.

title: Embedding, vector and model lineage
what: Lineage for derived artifacts: embeddings, features and models — what they were built from and when.
why: A model you cannot trace to its training data is a liability, not an asset.
when: Governing ML artifacts, features and their inputs.
read: Same rules as data lineage, plus version and owner on every artifact.
A feature with no recorded source is an assumption with a GPU bill.
pitfalls: Do not let "the pipeline" be a single anonymous box.
Do not version the model without versioning its inputs.
limits: Declared lineage; no evaluation of the models themselves (inference is out of scope by decision).

title: Data-product ownership and contracts
what: Who owns which data product, under which contract, with which consumers.
why: Every dataset that matters needs a name attached to it — the diagram is the accountability list.
when: Establishing or auditing data-product governance.
read: Owners are people or teams, never systems.
A contract without a named consumer is a wish, not a contract.
pitfalls: Do not list a team as owner when a person is accountable.
Do not let a product have zero consumers named — it is probably not a product.
limits: Governance documentation; the contracts are stated, not enforced.

title: Trust and data-handling boundaries
what: Trust zones and what may cross them: classification per zone, and the explicit gates between zones.
why: Security reviews fail on unstated boundaries; the diagram forces every crossing to have a name.
when: Threat modeling, compliance reviews, or designing data flows across trust levels.
read: Zones carry classification labels; every arrow crossing a zone edge is a gate with a rule.
Inside a zone, flows are routine; between zones, they are decisions.
pitfalls: Do not mark a boundary as trusted because it is inconvenient to gate.
Do not let a "temporary" bridge become the permanent path.
limits: Boundary documentation; no security evaluation or certification is implied.

title: Backup, restore and continuity design
what: Recovery structure: what is backed up, where copies live, and the restore path for each failure mode.
why: Backups nobody has restored are a hope; the restore path is the design.
when: Continuity planning and disaster-recovery reviews.
read: Read backwards from each failure mode to the copy that answers it.
RPO/RTO notes attach to the restore path, not the backup schedule.
pitfalls: Do not document a backup without its restore test.
Do not let one site hold both primary and only copy.
limits: Design documentation; no actual recovery is executed or timed here.

title: Current-to-target mapping
what: A migration map: current-state elements to target-state elements, with the transformation for each.
why: Migrations fail on unmapped items — the map is the proof nothing is silently dropped.
when: Any system, schema or platform migration.
read: Every current element has exactly one fate: migrated, transformed, retired or deferred.
A "temporary" parallel run is a phase with an exit date.
inputs: The fate and transformation of each
pitfalls: Do not leave an item unmapped because it is awkward.
Do not start the move before every row has a fate.
limits: Mapping documentation; the migration itself is not executed from this view.

title: Example-driven data-quality specification
what: Data-quality rules as examples: the checks a dataset must pass, stated against concrete records.
why: Rules stated on real examples get implemented; rules stated in prose get admired.
when: Defining acceptance for a data product or feed.
read: Each rule names the check, the records it guards, and what failure means.
A rule without a severity is an opinion.
pitfalls: Do not write rules you cannot point at a record for.
Do not make everything a warning — then nothing is.
limits: Specification documentation; the checks are stated, not executed by this view.

title: Linked diagrams and documentation views
what: Several views over one model: an overview with links into detail views at different audiences.
why: One model, many readers — the links keep every audience on the same facts.
when: Any documentation set where executives and implementers read the same system.
read: The overview is a map, not a simplification to maintain separately.
Detail views are selections of the same model — they cannot drift apart.
pitfalls: Do not maintain a separate "simplified" copy of the model.
Do not link to a view that no longer selects what the link promises.
limits: Composition documentation; navigation is a reading aid, not an application.

title: System context — C4-style
what: The system in its world: users, neighbouring systems, and the interactions at the boundary.
why: Every architecture conversation should be able to start on one page.
when: Introducing a system to anyone new — the first diagram of any review.
read: The system is one box; everything interesting is what touches it.
Arrows are responsibilities: who uses it for what, what it uses for what.
pitfalls: Do not show internals here — that is the container view's job.
Do not omit a dependency because it is "just a library".
limits: C4-style equivalent: the visual idiom, not a C4 certification.

title: Application/container responsibilities — C4-style
what: Inside the system: the deployable containers (apps, services, stores) and their responsibilities.
why: This is the map a new developer uses for the first week.
when: Onboarding, ownership reviews, deployment planning.
read: Each container owns a responsibility you can state in one line.
Connections name the protocol and direction, not just "talks to".
pitfalls: Do not list libraries as containers — they are not independently deployable.
Do not let a container have no stated responsibility.
limits: C4-style equivalent; deployment detail belongs to the deployment view.

title: Component responsibility map — C4-style
what: Inside one container: its components and how they collaborate.
why: This is where most day-to-day design discussion actually happens.
when: Designing or reviewing the inside of a service or application.
read: Components are code-level units with names you can find in the repo.
Collaborations read as "calls for purpose", not "uses".
pitfalls: Do not invent components that have no code counterpart.
Do not let every component talk to every other — that is a missing component.
limits: C4-style equivalent; not a code-structure certification.

title: Network/system topology
what: The physical/logical topology: hosts, buses and racks and how they attach.
why: Outages are read on topology first; this is the page you open at 3 a.m.
when: Infrastructure documentation and change windows.
read: Attachments declare where a host lives; the bus is shared, the rack is contained.
A host drawn without its attachment contract is decoration.
pitfalls: Do not draw the redundant path if you have not verified it exists.
Do not mix logical and physical layers without a label.
limits: Topology documentation; no monitoring or reachability is computed.

title: Network with icon pack symbols
what: The same topology drawn with the shipped network icon pack: routers, firewalls, load balancers, servers and access points as recognisable glyphs.
why: Symbols make a diagram read at a glance in a review — and they bind by default, so authors do not place them by hand.
when: Any network documentation meant for a mixed audience.
read: Glyphs are icon-pack bindings on ordinary nodes — the model is unchanged.
Per-node overrides exist for the cases the defaults do not cover.
inputs: The topology from the plain diagram
pitfalls: Do not treat an icon as a different element — it is the same node with a symbol.
Do not reach for a vendor pack — licensing keeps this set generic.
limits: Common-practice generic glyphs; no vendor artwork is included.

title: UML deployment diagram
what: Nodes, devices and execution environments as 3D boxes, with artifacts deployed on them and communication paths between.
why: Deployment is where architecture meets hardware; the 3D-box idiom keeps it readable.
when: Documenting what runs on which machine or environment.
read: Boxes inside boxes are nesting: an artifact has exactly one home node.
Communication paths are structural links, not runtime traffic.
pitfalls: Do not deploy an artifact to two homes without saying which is authoritative.
Do not draw network traffic as deployment.
limits: UML deployment notation; middleware-specific models and topology discovery are out of scope.

title: ISO 5807 flowchart — full symbol set
what: A flowchart using the complete ISO 5807 vocabulary: the classic symbols plus manual input, preparation, display, delay, loop limits, merge/extract, card, collate, sort and parallel mode.
why: Flowcharts are the most misused notation in the world — the full symbol set says exactly what each step is.
when: Documenting procedures for a general audience.
read: Read top to bottom following the arrows; every symbol has one meaning.
Decisions have exactly the branches their labels claim.
pitfalls: Do not use a process box for a decision (or vice versa).
Do not leave a branch unlabeled.
limits: Notation coverage of the ISO 5807 symbol set; no simulation of the procedure.

title: C4 deployment diagram
what: C4-style deployment: nodes and where the containers actually run.
why: The container view says what exists; the deployment view says where it lives.
when: Release planning, environment reviews, incident reading.
read: Placement is a fact per environment; paths between nodes are the links operations watches.
A container missing from the map is not deployed (or not documented).
pitfalls: Do not assume dev matches production on paper.
Do not hide a placement because it is embarrassing.
limits: C4-style equivalent with tag-chip styling; no live discovery.

title: C4 dynamic diagram (numbered messages)
what: One scenario as a numbered sequence of interactions between containers: who calls whom, in what order, for this story.
why: Static structure never shows order; a dynamic view answers "what actually happens when X".
when: Explaining a flow-through-scenario (login, checkout, failure handling).
read: Read the numbers in order — they are the story.
Each number is one interaction with a name and a direction.
pitfalls: Do not number interactions you have not traced.
Do not mix scenarios on one diagram.
limits: A recorded order, not a runtime trace; choreography conformance is out of scope.

title: UML sequence diagram with combined fragments
what: A full UML sequence diagram: lifelines, messages, combined fragments (alt/opt/loop), gates and time constraints.
why: Sequence diagrams are where protocol assumptions get written down and found out.
when: Specifying or reviewing message order between components.
read: Vertical position is time; fragments bracket the conditional parts.
A guard you cannot state in words does not belong on the diagram.
pitfalls: Do not use a fragment when you mean a separate diagram.
Do not leave a reply message unanswered without saying so.
limits: Notation coverage; interactions are trace descriptions, not executable models.

title: RACI responsibility matrix
what: Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each deliverable, one letter per person per row.
why: Accountability fails when it is shared; the matrix makes "exactly one A per row" something a validator can check.
when: Assigning work packages, approvals or escalation ownership.
read: Read row by row: each deliverable needs exactly one A.
R does the work, A answers for it, C is asked, I is told.
pitfalls: Do not allow two As on one row.
Do not confuse C (consulted before acting) with I (told after).
limits: Declared assignments with the one-accountable rule validated; the matrix does not enforce the work itself.

title: CRUD / data-access matrix
what: Which actor Creates, Reads, Updates and Deletes which entity — the access contract as a grid.
why: Access questions get answered at the cell instead of in a meeting.
when: Permission reviews, API design, or onboarding to a data model.
read: Read actor against entity: the letter is the permission.
An empty row is an inaccessible entity — deliberate or defect?
pitfalls: Do not write "admin" as the actor — name the role.
Do not leave D without an owner for retention questions.
limits: Declared permissions only; the grid is documentation, not an enforcement point.

title: General model-derived relationship matrix
what: Any two model lists crossed: elements on both axes, cells marking which pairs relate and how.
why: Cross-checks ("every X is covered by a Y") become visual gaps instead of list-diffing by hand.
when: Coverage checks: capabilities↔systems, requirements↔tests, teams↔systems.
read: Rows are one model list, columns another; a marked cell means the pair relates.
An empty row or column is the finding: something relates to nothing.
inputs: The mark each true cell carries
pitfalls: Do not fill cells to look complete — an honest empty cell is the finding.
Do not mix relationship types in one mark without a legend.
limits: Model-derived marks; the matrix reports the model, it does not prove coverage in reality.

title: Source-bound record table
what: Model records rendered as a literal rows-and-columns table — the data itself, formatted, not a chart.
why: Some reviews need the numbers, not the picture; the table is the honest projection.
when: Reconciliation, sign-off, or checking exact values a chart would round.
read: Columns are the record fields, in declared order.
Missing values print as missing — never zero-filled.
pitfalls: Do not sort the table in the picture instead of the source.
Do not read a formatted unit as a different unit.
limits: Presentation of declared records; no aggregation beyond what the view declares.

title: Typed decision table — unique match
what: A typed decision table where exactly one rule may match any input: overlapping conditions are defects, not style.
why: Uniqueness is the strongest review contract a rule set can carry — any ambiguity fails loudly.
when: Rules that must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive (fee codes, eligibility).
read: Every input hits exactly one row — or the table is broken.
Type domains on inputs define what "match" may claim.
pitfalls: Do not write two rows that can both be true.
Do not leave a domain hole: unique also requires complete.
limits: Bounded evaluation against one input record; no arbitrary rule-language execution.

title: Typed decision table — collect matches
what: A decision table where every matching rule contributes to the outcome: collect, then aggregate.
why: Some policies are additive by design — the collect policy makes the accumulation explicit instead of hidden in code.
when: Scoring, surcharges, risk points — anything summed across matching rules.
read: Read all rows: every match counts, not the first.
The aggregation (sum/min/max/count) is declared on the table, not implied.
pitfalls: Do not add a rule whose points you cannot justify independently.
Do not read collect order as priority — it is a bag, not a race.
limits: Bounded evaluation against one input record with the declared aggregation.

title: Numeric heatmap
what: A grid where cell colour encodes a numeric measure: magnitude at a glance across two axes.
why: Outliers hide in tables and shout in heatmaps.
when: Load, cost, error or latency across services and time windows.
read: Colour is the number — darker/hotter means larger.
Read the scale first: the same colour means different numbers on different maps.
pitfalls: Do not compare colours across heatmaps with different scales.
Do not let one extreme cell flatten the rest of the scale.
limits: Declared scale from declared data; no automatic outlier detection.

title: Risk/priority matrix with threshold bands
what: A heatmap whose colours come from declared thresholds: green/amber/red by band, not by raw magnitude.
why: Reviewers ask "is it bad?" before "how big?" — bands answer the first question without hiding the second.
when: Risk registers, SLO dashboards, priority triage.
read: Band boundaries are data, declared in the view — read them before the colours.
A cell near a boundary is a judgement call, not a colour.
pitfalls: Do not tune a threshold to make a cell change colour without saying so.
Do not use red/green without a non-colour cue.
limits: Declared bands from declared data; the thresholds are policy, not statistics.

title: Categorical status matrix
what: A status board: cells coloured by category (ok/degraded/down/unknown) rather than number.
why: One glance answers "what is on fire" across many small services.
when: Operations walls and release readiness boards.
read: Categories are declared sets with declared colours.
Unknown is a category, not a colour to ignore.
pitfalls: Do not add a category without a colour and a meaning.
Do not let stale data look fresh — timestamp the board.
limits: Declared categories from declared data; no live probing.

title: SWOT and four-panel strategic analysis
what: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats in four quadrants — the classic strategy frame as records.
why: The frame forces balance: an analysis that is all strengths or all threats shows immediately.
when: Strategy workshops and decision framing.
read: Internal factors above, external below (or per the quadrant labels).
Each entry is a claim with an owner, not a mood.
pitfalls: Do not park weaknesses in opportunities to avoid the conversation.
Do not run a SWOT with no decision attached to it.
limits: A framing tool: entries are declared content, no scoring or recommendation is computed.

title: SIPOC process overview
what: Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers as one row-oriented summary: the 30-second version of a process.
why: Before any detail diagram, SIPOC aligns everyone on scope and boundaries.
when: Opening a process-improvement or documentation effort.
read: Read left to right: who supplies, what arrives, what happens, what leaves, who receives.
The process column is a handful of verbs, not the detail diagram.
pitfalls: Do not write the whole flowchart in the process column.
Do not forget the customer of the output.
limits: Summary frame only; detail belongs to the flowchart or DFD.

title: Customer/service journey panels
what: A journey map: stages across the top, touchpoints and experience below.
why: The map makes the worst moment findable instead of average-scored away.
when: Service design and customer-experience reviews.
read: Read stage by stage: what the customer does, feels and hits.
The dip in the curve is a named moment, not a mood.
pitfalls: Do not average the curve — it hides the moment that loses the customer.
Do not map the company's process instead of the customer's journey.
limits: Declared journey content; no measurement pipeline is attached.

title: Empathy map and balanced scorecard
what: An empathy map — what a user says, thinks, does and feels — plus a scorecard variant in the same source.
why: The four-quadrant map keeps a team from designing for itself.
when: Early discovery for a feature or service.
read: Quadrants are observation categories, not personality types.
Entries are evidence or declared hypotheses — mark which.
pitfalls: Do not present a hypothesis as an observation.
Do not run an empathy session about a demographic instead of a person.
limits: Declared empathy content; the map organises evidence, it does not collect it.

title: Story map
what: A story map: user activities across the top, stories beneath, releases sliced horizontally.
why: It keeps the walking skeleton visible while the backlog grows.
when: Release planning for a user-facing product.
read: Top row is the user's day; below is what we build, sliced by release.
A story above the release line ships; below it waits.
pitfalls: Do not slice releases by component — slice by user outcome.
Do not let the top row become a feature list.
limits: Declared map content; no estimation or velocity is computed.

title: Line chart
what: A data-bound line chart: an ordered series over an ordered axis, from declared records.
why: Trend is the question lines answer best — and the records behind the line stay inspectable.
when: Anything over time or another ordered axis.
read: The axis order comes from the data, not the alphabet.
A line connects consecutive points — it is not a regression.
pitfalls: Do not draw a line across a gap as if it were measured.
Do not read slope without reading the axis scale.
limits: Declared records and bounded native marks; no trend computation.

title: Area chart
what: A filled series: the line plus the weight of what is under it.
why: When volume matters as much as direction, the filled form says both.
when: Totals evolving: throughput, stock, energy.
read: The top edge is the value; the fill is emphasis, not a second series.
Stacked areas read as composition — this one reads as one series.
pitfalls: Do not fill a series that can go negative without saying where zero is.
Do not read the filled area as a probability.
limits: Declared records; bounded native marks.

title: Pie and doughnut charts
what: Shares of a total as slices of a circle — and the doughnut variant with its centre free for the total.
why: Composition reads instantly when there are few slices and a real whole.
when: Parts of one meaningful total (market share, budget split).
read: Slices sum to the whole — percentages are computed from the records.
The doughnut's centre carries the total, not a decoration.
pitfalls: Do not use a pie for values that are not parts of a total.
Do not ship seven-plus slices — group the tail.
limits: Declared records; percentages derive from them, never from hand-entered numbers.

title: Scatter and perceptual plots
what: Points in two dimensions: correlation, clusters and outliers from declared records.
why: Averages hide structure that only the cloud shows.
when: Exploring relationships between two measures.
read: Each point is one record on two axes.
A cluster is a hypothesis to investigate, not a conclusion.
pitfalls: Do not read correlation as causation.
Do not crop an outlier out of the frame silently.
limits: Declared points; no regression or clustering is computed by this view.

title: Calendar-ordered time-series
what: A series on a real calendar axis: dates are data, spacing is honest.
why: Equal spacing for unequal time gaps is the most common chart lie; the calendar axis removes it.
when: Anything timestamped: metrics, events, activity.
read: Gaps on the axis are gaps in time, not missing pixels.
Read the timezone note before comparing days.
pitfalls: Do not resample silently — the axis shows what was recorded.
Do not compare series on different time axes.
limits: Declared timestamps and bounded marks; no forecasting.

title: Grouped multi-series bars
what: Several series side by side per category: comparison across groups without stacking.
why: Side-by-side is the honest comparison when absolute values matter more than composition.
when: This period vs last, plan vs actual, per team or product.
read: Same colour means same series across groups.
Read per group first, then across groups within one series.
pitfalls: Do not group more series than the eye can separate.
Do not let one tall group squash the rest of the scale.
limits: Declared records; bounded native marks.

title: Signed stacked bars
what: Composition per category as stacked segments, including negative contributions across zero.
why: Part-to-whole with a baseline: gains above, losses below.
when: Budget vs variance, contribution breakdowns, reconciliations.
read: Segments stack from the zero line out, in declared series order.
The total is the stack height, not a separate mark.
pitfalls: Do not stack things that are not additive.
Do not hide the zero line when signs mix.
limits: Declared records; bounded native marks.

title: Percentage-stacked bars
what: Each bar normalised to 100%: composition comparison across categories of different sizes.
why: When the mix matters more than the mass, normalising removes the size argument.
when: Share of type/status per category across unequal categories.
read: Every bar is 100% — compare segment shares, not heights.
Percentages derive from the records, never from entered numbers.
pitfalls: Do not forget the small category whose 40% is 3 records.
Do not mix absolute and percentage bars on one chart.
limits: Declared records; normalisation is computed from them.

title: Multiple-line chart
what: Several series as overlaid lines on one axis: trend comparison without stacking.
why: Overlay is the honest way to compare trajectories that should not be added.
when: KPIs per service, per cohort, per period.
read: Colour is the series; the legend is the contract.
Lines cross freely — crossing is not interaction.
pitfalls: Do not overlay more lines than colours can distinguish.
Do not give two series the same name on different scales.
limits: Declared records; bounded native marks.

title: Multiple-series area chart
what: Several series as stacked areas: composition of a total over an ordered axis.
why: Shows both the total trajectory and who contributes to it.
when: Load, cost or traffic broken down by source over time.
read: The top edge is the total; the bands are the parts, in declared order.
A band swallowing another is data, not a rendering bug.
pitfalls: Do not stack series that are not parts of one whole.
Do not put the volatile series at the bottom where it wobbles everything.
limits: Declared records; bounded native marks.

title: Actual versus target / layered marks
what: Measured values and supplied target marks on one scale: bars for actual, a line for the declared target.
why: Performance against a requirement is visible, and the target's provenance stays inspectable.
when: Comparative quality and operations reports.
read: The target is a separate source fact, not a computed decoration.
Layers are declared per series: which mark plays which role.
inputs: The target series and where it came from
pitfalls: A target line is not a statistical control limit.
Do not change the target by dragging a line — change the record.
limits: Finite arithmetic and bounded marks; no independent multi-unit axes.

title: Histogram — counts and density
what: A distribution as binned counts (and the density variant): how values spread, not just their average.
why: The average is where histograms go to hide the truth.
when: Latency, sizes, scores — anything with a shape worth seeing.
read: Bins are declared intervals with inclusive/exclusive edges noted.
Counts and density answer different questions — switch variants to see.
pitfalls: Do not tune bin count to hide a second mode.
Do not read a density curve as more data than the records hold.
limits: Exact bin counts from the records; boundary inclusion is declared and tested.

title: Pareto chart
what: Categories sorted by count descending, with the cumulative share line: the vital few versus the trivial many.
why: It tells you which three fixes kill most of the problem.
when: Defect triage, incident categories, complaint analysis.
read: Bars descend left to right; the line is cumulative share.
The 80% mark is a reading aid, not a law.
pitfalls: Do not sort by anything but count — that is the point.
Do not merge the tail into "other" without a label.
limits: Declared counts; the cumulative line derives from them.

title: Waterfall / running-change reconciliation
what: A running total built step by step: start, deltas up and down, end — the reconciliation made visible.
why: Executives read "how did we get from A to B" better in steps than in a table of deltas.
when: Bridging two totals: budgets, headcount, inventory.
read: Each block starts where the last ended; up is green, down is red by convention.
The final block must equal the end total — the chart reconciles or it is wrong.
pitfalls: Do not reorder deltas for drama — the story is in the declared order.
Do not leave a step unexplained.
limits: Declared deltas; the running total derives from them.

title: Box plot conventions
what: Distribution summaries as boxes: median, quartiles, whiskers and outliers — Tukey and min/max conventions side by side.
why: Five numbers per group beat one average per group, every time.
when: Comparing spreads across groups or versions.
read: The box is the middle half; whiskers follow the declared rule (1.5×IQR or min/max).
Outlier dots are records, named by the rule that flagged them.
pitfalls: Do not mix conventions without a label — switch variants to see why it matters.
Do not read the median as the mean.
limits: Exact quartiles from the records; the R7 rule and outlier set are declared and tested.

title: Distribution chart pack
what: The distribution family beyond the histogram: violin shapes, density curves, Q-Q plots and quantile dots from one record set.
why: Shape questions need shape tools — each of these shows what averages and even histograms smooth away.
when: Comparing distributions, checking normality, reading tails.
read: The violin mirrors the density; the Q-Q compares against the theoretical line.
Quantile dots are records, never a smoothed invention.
inputs: The comparison target (normal, or another group)
The variant that answers your question
pitfalls: Do not read a KDE bandwidth as data.
Do not conclude normality from a pretty Q-Q alone.
limits: Declared kernels and quantiles from the records; no significance testing.

title: Tree and radial chart pack
what: Hierarchies as nested area: sunbursts, tidy/radial trees, circle packing and packed bubbles from one hierarchy.
why: Nested magnitude reads differently in each form — the pack lets the data pick the right one.
when: Org size, budget trees, file storage, taxonomy size.
read: Area is value, nesting is structure.
Read outward (sunburst) or along branches (trees) — never compare area across different forms directly.
pitfalls: Do not force deep hierarchies into a sunburst — they become confetti.
Do not compare sibling sizes across separate charts.
limits: Declared hierarchy and values; layout is deterministic per form.

title: Grid and network chart pack
what: Grid-based charts: heatmaps, calendar maps, parallel coordinates and word clouds from declared records.
why: Patterns across many cells, days or dimensions need a grid, not another line.
when: Activity over days, many-metric comparison, term frequency.
read: Cells are records; colour encodes the declared measure.
Parallel coordinates read as profiles per record, not as trends.
pitfalls: Do not read a word cloud as precise frequency — it is emphasis.
Do not compare cell colours across differently scaled maps.
limits: Declared records; no clustering or correlation is computed.

title: Statistical overlays (error bars, regression, loess)
what: Marks plus statistics: error bars on declared uncertainty, regression and loess lines fitted to the records.
why: The overlay separates the measured fact from the fitted model — and says which is which.
when: Reporting measurements with uncertainty or trend models.
read: Points are records; the line is a model of them, named with its method.
Error bars are declared ranges, not computed guesses — unless the view declares the computation.
pitfalls: Do not show a fit without naming its method.
Do not let the line outrun the points it claims to summarise.
limits: Declared fits from declared data; no confidence interval is invented.

title: Gantt / supplied-date schedule
what: A schedule from supplied dates: bars per task on a calendar, dependencies as links.
why: Dates are data — a Gantt you can edit in source stays honest when the plan moves.
when: Any dated plan small enough to read on one page.
read: Bars are declared spans, not estimates the chart invented.
A dependency arrow is finish-to-start; it constrains reading, not the calendar.
pitfalls: Do not schedule a task before its predecessor without a note.
Do not let the chart silently shift dates — every date is in the source.
limits: Supplied dates only; no scheduling algorithm runs.

title: Composed dashboard / report page
what: Several views composed on one page: charts, tables and a graph sharing one model and one data block.
why: The dashboard is the summary stakeholders actually read — and it refreshes as one transaction, not nine.
when: Periodic operations and quality reporting.
read: Panels are views of the same records — a number that disagrees with its chart is a defect, not a refresh lag.
Composition is one level deep, by rule.
pitfalls: Do not nest a dashboard in a dashboard.
Do not add a panel that answers a question nobody asked.
limits: One composition level with per-panel budgets; refresh swaps records atomically.

title: Lifecycle trace verification
what: A flat lifecycle diagram plus its trace checker: replay a declared event list through the states and verify the outcome.
why: The state machine you cannot run an event list through is a picture, not a contract.
when: Checking that a declared lifecycle actually reaches the states its name implies.
read: States and transitions are the model; the trace is a recorded input you replay.
A mismatch names the event and the expected state.
pitfalls: Do not treat a passing trace as proof of all traces.
Do not hide an event the machine cannot consume.
limits: Deterministic flat-lifecycle replay with exactly-one-transition validation.

title: Yourdon-style DFD
what: A data-flow diagram in the Yourdon idiom: circles for processes, open boxes for stores, named arrows for flows.
why: The idiom keeps flows honest: every arrow carries data, every process transforms some.
when: Classic systems analysis and documentation.
read: Processes are verbs, stores are nouns at rest, entities are outside the system.
Balancing: a decomposed process shows the same boundary flows as its parent.
pitfalls: Do not draw control signals as data flows.
Do not decompose a process and lose a flow at the boundary.
limits: The Yourdon idiom as notation; balancing is a modeling discipline, not a validator here.

title: Gane–Sarson-style DFD
what: The Gane–Sarson DFD variant: rounded process boxes, parallel-line stores, and the same discipline of named data flows.
why: Some organisations standardised on Gane–Sarson; the variant exists so the document reads natively to them.
when: DFD work in Gane–Sarson shops.
read: Same rules as Yourdon — only the silhouettes differ.
Stores are the parallel lines; everything else maps one to one.
inputs: The same content as any DFD
pitfalls: Do not mix Yourdon and Gane–Sarson symbols in one diagram.
Do not read the variant as a different model.
limits: The Gane–Sarson idiom as notation; the same underlying model as any DFD.

title: UML class diagram — associations and classifiers
what: Classes with typed attributes and operations, association ends with multiplicities, navigability and aggregation.
why: The class diagram is the shared vocabulary between domain talk and code — multiplicities make the rules checkable.
when: Object-oriented design, domain modelling, or any review of "what has what, how many, owned by whom".
read: Boxes are classifiers; compartments hold attributes and operations.
Read each association end: multiplicity, role name, navigability — each is a separate claim.
pitfalls: Do not leave multiplicity off an end "for now" — it is the claim.
Do not model a relationship attribute without an association class or a home.
limits: Declared structure with UML semantics validated; no code generation or behavioural check is implied.

title: UML object diagram — instance snapshot
what: Instances at a moment: objects with slot values linked as the classifiers permit — a snapshot, not a schema.
why: One concrete snapshot falsifies a wrong class diagram faster than an hour of abstract review.
when: Testing a class model against a real example, or documenting a known configuration.
read: Underlined instance:Classifier names are objects; slots show current values.
Links are instances of associations — check them against the class diagram.
pitfalls: Do not invent a link the class model forbids.
A snapshot shows one moment — do not read it as the only state.
limits: Declared instances; conformance to a class model is documented, not re-derived here.

title: UML component and composite structure
what: Components wired through provided and required ports, and the internal parts-and-connectors view of a structured classifier.
why: Ports make interfaces explicit — the diagram says what may connect to what before the wiring exists.
when: Component architecture, integration design, or explaining how a big part is built from smaller ones.
read: Ball-and-socket pairs are provided/required interfaces; assembly connectors join compatible pairs.
In the structures variant, parts inside the boundary play roles in the whole.
pitfalls: Do not connect a required interface to another required one.
A port without an interface type is a wish, not a contract.
limits: Declared structure with port compatibility validated; no deployment or runtime wiring is implied.

title: UML package and profile diagrams
what: Packages grouping model elements with imports and merges, and profiles declaring stereotypes that extend the metamodel.
why: Large models fail at the boundaries between teams; packages declare those boundaries and who depends on them.
when: Partitioning a big model, or documenting a domain-specific UML extension.
read: A folder shape is a package; dashed arrows are imports/merges with direction.
In the profile variant, stereotypes and tagged values extend, never replace, the base metaclass.
inputs: The relevant UML package or profile definitions
pitfalls: Do not let imports form a cycle — that is one package wearing two hats.
A stereotype without a base metaclass is undefined.
limits: Declared packaging and profiling; element ownership is validated, code packaging is not implied.

title: UML state machine — pseudostates and composite states
what: States, transitions with triggers/guards/effects, plus the full pseudostate vocabulary: initial, choice, junction, history, entry/exit points.
why: State machines make "what may happen next" enumerable — reviewers can ask about every missing transition.
when: Lifecycle-heavy objects: orders, connections, approvals, devices.
read: Rounded boxes are states; arrows are transitions labelled trigger [guard] / effect.
Filled circles and diamonds are pseudostates — routing, not resting places.
pitfalls: Do not leave a state with no path out unless it is final by intent.
Do not put work in a pseudostate — effects belong on transitions.
limits: Declared machine with well-formedness validation; no code execution or model checking is claimed.

title: UML activity — pins, decisions and interrupts
what: Actions wired by object and control flow: pins as typed ports on actions, decision/merge diamonds, fork/join bars, interruptible regions.
why: The activity diagram is where "the process" becomes checkable: every input must come from somewhere.
when: Detailing an algorithm or business process one level below a use case.
read: Rounded boxes are actions; small squares on their edges are pins (typed inputs/outputs).
Diamonds decide or merge; thick bars fork and rejoin concurrent flow.
pitfalls: Do not leave a required pin unfed — the validator treats it as the defect it is.
Merge and decision are different diamonds; do not swap them.
limits: Declared flow with pin and region validation; no execution or simulation is performed.

title: Activity partitions (swimlanes)
what: An activity diagram whose actions sit in named partitions — one lane per role or system that owns the work.
why: Most process disputes are ownership disputes; lanes make the handoffs (and their number) visible.
when: Cross-team processes where "who does this step" matters as much as the step.
read: Each lane is a responsible party; arrows crossing a lane boundary are handoffs.
Count the crossings — each one is a delay and a failure mode.
pitfalls: Do not put one step in two lanes — split it at the handoff.
A lane that only receives work is a queue, and should be drawn as one.
limits: Declared partitions and flow; organisational truth is documented, not enforced.

title: UML communication diagram
what: Objects as nodes, links as edges, numbered messages along the links — the sequence diagram rearranged around structure.
why: When the wiring matters more than the timeline, the communication layout shows who talks to whom at a glance.
when: Reviewing collaboration structure: integration maps, object networks, message fan-out.
read: Boxes are participants; lines are links; numbered labels are messages in call order (1, 1.1, 1.2 …).
Nesting in the numbers is nesting in the calls.
pitfalls: Do not skip the sequence numbers — without them the diagram has no order.
A message on no link is a topology error, not a style choice.
limits: Declared participants and message order; no protocol conformance or timing is claimed.

title: UML interaction overview
what: An activity diagram whose actions are whole interactions — sequence fragments composed with decision and flow.
why: It is the map of the maps: each node opens into a full interaction, so reviews can zoom without losing the route.
when: Systems with several scenario diagrams that need one navigable composition.
read: Frames labelled ref are references to other interactions; the flow between them is the overview.
Variants open the referenced detail diagrams.
pitfalls: Do not inline a full sequence here — reference it, or the overview stops being one.
Every referenced fragment must exist; a dangling ref is a defect.
limits: Declared composition of declared interactions; cross-diagram behavioural consistency is not proved.

title: UML timing diagram
what: Lifelines as state waveforms over a shared time axis, with duration and time constraints marked.
why: Some contracts live in the fourth dimension; the timing diagram is the only UML view that draws them directly.
when: Real-time behaviour, protocol timing, SLA-shaped constraints.
read: Each row is one lifeline; the step line is its state over time.
Braces and arrows annotate durations — they are constraints, not measurements.
pitfalls: Do not mix scales between rows without saying so.
A constraint with no units is an argument waiting to happen.
limits: Declared timing with constraint validation; no simulation or schedulability analysis is performed.

title: BPMN process and collaboration
what: Pools and lanes with tasks, gateways and events wired by sequence flow; the collaboration variant adds message flow between pools.
why: BPMN is the one process notation both the business and the workflow engine read — ambiguities surface as gateway questions.
when: Any process that crosses team or system boundaries and needs an executable-adjacent reading.
read: Sequence flow stays inside a pool; message flow crosses between pools.
Gateway diamonds branch and join — read the gateway type marker before the labels.
inputs: The events that start and end paths
pitfalls: Do not draw sequence flow between pools — that is what message flow is for.
A gateway without a default path deadlocks on the unlisted case.
limits: Declared BPMN with structural validation; no engine deployment or execution semantics are claimed.

title: BPMN choreography
what: Interactions as first-class tasks: each choreography task names the initiating and receiving participants in its bands.
why: When no party owns the process, the contract is the sequence of exchanges itself — the choreography draws exactly that.
when: Cross-organisation protocols: ordering, settlement, any dance with no conductor.
read: Each task is one exchange; the shaded band is the receiver, the light band initiates.
Sequence flow orders the exchanges, not internal steps — internals live in each party's own process.
pitfalls: Do not model one party's internal steps here — that is a process diagram's job.
The initiator band must be the sender of the first message in the exchange.
limits: Declared choreography with participant-band validation; enforcement between organisations is out of scope.

title: CMMN case model
what: A case: stages, tasks and milestones inside a case file, with sentries guarding what may start when.
why: Knowledge work does not flow in a straight line; CMMN models the available moves and their enabling conditions instead.
when: Cases — claims, incidents, applications — where order emerges from conditions, not a fixed route.
read: The folder frame is the case; stages group the work; milestones are achievements, not tasks.
Diamond sentries on an entry criterion say "this may start when …".
pitfalls: Do not wire everything with sequence flow — CMMN's point is conditional availability.
A milestone with no criterion is a hope, not a checkpoint.
limits: Declared case model with structural validation; no case-engine execution is claimed.

title: SysML block definition diagram
what: Blocks, their properties (parts, values, references) and the relationships between blocks: composition, generalisation, association.
why: The BDD is the system's nouns and their structure — every other SysML view hangs off these definitions.
when: Systems architecture decomposition, from vehicle-scale down to a single assembly.
read: Blocks are boxes with compartments; filled-diamond lines are composition (owned parts).
Read multiplicities on part ends — they bound the internal block diagram.
pitfalls: Do not confuse composition (part-of, one owner) with reference (used-by).
A part with no multiplicity is an under-specified IBD waiting to happen.
limits: Declared structure with SysML well-formedness validation; no analysis or simulation is implied.

title: SysML internal block diagram
what: Inside one block: its parts wired through ports, connectors carrying the declared item flows.
why: The IBD is where interface mismatches are found on paper — every connector crosses a port that must type-check.
when: Detailing how the parts of one assembly connect and what flows between them.
read: The frame is the enclosing block; rectangles inside are parts named role:Type.
Small squares on part borders are ports; connectors between ports carry items.
pitfalls: Do not connect parts without ports once ports are declared — the hidden interface is the bug.
A connector carrying an item the port cannot convey is a defect, not documentation.
limits: Declared connectivity with port compatibility validation; physical routing is not modelled.

title: SysML parametric diagram
what: Constraint blocks (equations) bound to the value properties of blocks — the system's arithmetic made explicit.
why: Performance claims stop being adjectives when the balance equations are drawn and bound to real properties.
when: Trade studies: mass, power, flow, cost — any "the numbers must add up" argument.
read: Rounded boxes are constraint properties (equations); small circles are parameters bound to values.
Binding connectors wire equation parameters to block value properties.
pitfalls: Do not leave a parameter unbound — an equation with a free variable checks nothing.
Units are part of the property; a binding across unit systems is a defect.
limits: Declared constraints and bindings; solving or simulating the equations is out of scope.

title: SysML requirements diagram
what: Requirements with id and text, wired by satisfy/verify/derive/refine relationships to the model elements that answer them.
why: A requirement with no satisfy link is a wish; a design element traced to no requirement is a luxury — the diagram shows both.
when: Contract-driven development, compliance arguments, coverage reviews.
read: Boxes labelled «requirement» carry the id and text; dashed arrows are the trace relationships, read with their keywords.
A verify link must end at a test case; a satisfy link at a design element.
pitfalls: Do not paraphrase requirement text in the box — quote it, or the trace is to your summary.
Refine is not satisfy: refine clarifies, satisfy answers.
limits: Declared traceability with relationship-type validation; coverage is shown, not certified.

title: DMN decision requirements diagram
what: Decisions, input data and knowledge sources as nodes; information-requirement arrows saying what each decision needs.
why: The DRD is the table of contents for the decision logic — reviewers can demand to see every input's source.
when: Before writing the decision tables: agree what is decided from what.
read: Rectangles are decisions, ovals are input data; arrows point from requirement to the decision that requires it.
Variants open the actual decision tables behind two of the decisions.
pitfalls: Do not let a decision read data that never enters the diagram.
A decision nobody requires is dead logic — delete it or wire its consumer.
limits: Declared requirements graph with reference validation; the tables' logic is validated separately (see the decision-table chapters).

title: SoaML service architecture
what: Participants offering and consuming services through service contracts — the architecture of who serves whom.
why: Service landscapes rot by assumption; SoaML makes the contracts and their consumers a drawable, checkable graph.
when: Service inventory design, API landscape reviews, consumer-provider onboarding.
read: Participants are the parties; service interfaces (ball/socket style) attach contracts to ports.
The choreography variant shows the message order the contract permits.
inputs: Who provides and who consumes each
pitfalls: Do not draw a consumer wired to a provider without the contract between them.
A contract with no choreography is underspecified — the variant shows why.
limits: Declared architecture with contract-attachment validation; runtime governance is out of scope.

title: UAF strategic viewpoint (St)
what: The UAF Strategic viewpoint: enterprise phases, capabilities and the strategic map that says which capability arrives when.
why: Portfolio arguments need a picture where capability gaps are visible before they are budget lines.
when: Enterprise architecture roadmapping and capability planning.
read: Rows and columns follow the declared strategic taxonomy; each cell/box is a capability or phase claim.
Trace from a capability to the phases that deliver it before agreeing dates.
pitfalls: Do not promise a capability in a phase with no project behind it.
A capability with no owner is a slide, not a plan.
limits: Declared strategic model with UAF profile validation; portfolio feasibility is not assessed.

title: UAF summary and overview (S&O)
what: The Summary & Overview viewpoint: the executive one-pager framing the architecture — purpose, scope, key elements in one pictogram.
why: Every viewpoint set needs a front page that says what the architecture is for and which views answer which questions.
when: First artifact of any UAF description; the review-meeting opener.
read: The frame is the overview; members are the key architectural elements selected for the summary.
Read it as a map to the other viewpoints, not a replacement for them.
pitfalls: Do not crowd the overview — it is a signpost, not the territory.
An element in the frame must exist in the model; a decorative box is a lie.
limits: Declared summary frame over a declared model; completeness of the selection is a review judgement.

title: MSC / HMSC message sequence chart
what: ITU message sequence charts: instances as vertical axes, messages as arrows between them, with an HMSC referencing sub-charts.
why: Protocol reviews need the exact interleaving on paper; MSC is the telecom-standard way to draw it.
when: Protocol specification, inter-system message contracts, telecom and embedded documentation.
read: Each vertical line is an instance axis; time runs downward.
Arrows between axes are messages; the variant shows a high-level MSC referencing the details.
pitfalls: Do not cross arrows casually — crossing is a claim about overtaking.
A referenced sub-chart must exist; a dangling ref fails review.
limits: Declared charts with MSC structural validation; no conformance test against an implementation is run.

title: SDL system and process
what: ITU SDL: the system as blocks and channels, and inside a process the state machine with input, task, output and decision symbols.
why: SDL pairs the structural channels with the behavioural states in one standard — the two views check each other.
when: Telecom and reactive-system documentation where signal protocols meet state behaviour.
read: In the system view, blocks exchange signals over named channels.
In the process variant, read top-down: start, input, task/decision, output, next state.
pitfalls: Do not send a signal over a channel that does not carry it.
Every decision branch needs a continuation; an unhandled input is a stuck process.
limits: Declared SDL with structural validation; no code generation or exhaustive simulation is claimed.

title: IEC 61131-3 function block diagram
what: Function blocks wired input-to-output: typed pins, feedback paths, the dataflow reading of control logic.
why: Control engineers read dataflow, not ladder rails; the FBD is the same logic drawn as a circuit of blocks.
when: Process-control documentation, interlock logic, any block-and-wire control review.
read: Blocks compute; pins are typed inputs and outputs; wires carry values left to right except feedback.
Read feedback loops deliberately — they are state, and reviewers must find them.
pitfalls: Do not wire an output to an output.
A feedback loop without a memory block is an algebraic loop — say where the state lives.
limits: Declared FBD with pin-type validation; no PLC compilation or scan-cycle simulation is performed.

title: Petri net
what: Places, transitions, tokens: the producer/consumer net with the marking drawn, firing rules implicit in the topology.
why: Concurrency questions (can this deadlock? can this starve?) have a formal home — and it draws small.
when: Reasoning about concurrent resource flow: pipelines, buffers, locks, work queues.
read: Circles are places (holding tokens), bars are transitions (firing), dots are the current marking.
A transition fires when every input place holds a token — trace one firing by hand.
pitfalls: Do not draw an arc transition-to-transition — flow alternates place/transition.
An empty net proves nothing; declare the marking you are analysing.
limits: Declared net with structural validation; reachability and liveness are reading aids here, not a model-checker run.

title: ORM fact model
what: Object-Role Modeling: entity types, value types and the fact roles between them, with uniqueness and mandatory constraints drawn on the roles.
why: ORM verbalises facts in sentences non-modellers can confirm, and the constraints are drawn where they apply.
when: Deep domain modelling where every constraint must survive a business review.
read: Ellipses are object types; boxes on the fact lines are roles — read a fact as a sentence across the roles.
Bars over roles are uniqueness constraints; dots are mandatory — each is a separate, checkable claim.
pitfalls: Do not model a ternary fact as two binaries — the constraint semantics differ.
A role with no uniqueness reading is an unfinished sentence.
limits: Declared fact model with constraint validation; schema generation is a separate step, not claimed here.

title: Value stream map — current state
what: A lean value stream: process boxes with data, inventory triangles between them, information flow above, the timeline ladder below.
why: Lead time hides in the gaps between processes; the map adds up processing time versus waiting time on one page.
when: Lean improvement: before any kaizen, draw the current state as measured.
read: Process boxes run left to right; triangles are inventory (waiting) between them.
The ladder at the bottom separates value-adding time from waiting — the ratio is the point.
inputs: The process steps with measured times
The information flow that triggers work
pitfalls: Do not draw the future state first — a map of wishes improves nothing.
Times are measurements, not targets; mark estimates honestly.
limits: Declared map with VSM symbol validation; the arithmetic of the timeline is shown from declared numbers, not re-measured.

title: VSM symbol library
what: The value-stream-mapping symbol set on one sheet: processes, inventories, flows, kaizen bursts and information icons.
why: A shared symbol sheet ends the "what does that triangle mean" detour in every mapping workshop.
when: Reference while drawing or reviewing any value stream map.
read: Each symbol is labelled with its VSM name; find the mark from your map and read its meaning here.
Symbols are drawn at working size — what you see is what renders in a real map.
inputs: None — this is a reference sheet
pitfalls: Do not invent private symbols when the standard set covers the case.
Do not mix icon styles inside one map.
limits: The declared symbol library; meanings follow common VSM practice, no external certification implied.

title: IDEF0 function model
what: Functions as boxes with ICOM arrows: inputs in the left, controls over the top, outputs right, mechanisms below — decomposed level by level.
why: ICOM sides force the question most process diagrams skip: what constrains this, and what performs it?
when: Function analysis in regulated or defence-adjacent programmes, or any "what does the system do" baseline.
read: The context view is the single A-0 box; the variant decomposes it into numbered child functions.
Arrows are labelled nouns; the side they enter is the role they play.
pitfalls: Do not let an arrow change sides between levels without a tunnel declaration.
Every parent ICOM must appear (or be deliberately consumed) in the children.
limits: Declared model with ICOM-side validation; conformance certification to the IDEF0 standard is not implied.

title: PERT / CPM network
what: Activities as a dependency network with durations — the critical path read off the longest chain.
why: Schedule risk lives on the critical path; the network makes "what slips the date" a computable question.
when: Project planning where dependencies, not calendars, drive the end date.
read: Nodes/boxes are activities with durations; arrows are finish-to-start dependencies.
The longest path is the critical one — any delay on it moves the end date one-for-one.
pitfalls: Do not add a dependency to force a resource fit — that is a resource problem wearing a logic costume.
A cycle in the network is a planning error, not a paradox.
limits: Declared network; path arithmetic follows the declared durations, estimation method is yours to document.

title: Fault tree and event tree
what: Top-down fault logic (AND/OR gates to basic events) and the forward event tree from an initiating event through safety functions.
why: Safety arguments must be enumerable: every path to the hazard drawn, every barrier after the initiator named.
when: Hazard analysis, reliability reviews, safety-case documentation.
read: Fault tree: read downward from the top event through gates to basic events; AND gates need all inputs, OR needs one.
Event tree variant: read left to right — each branch point is a safety function succeeding or failing.
pitfalls: Do not hide a common cause in two "independent" branches.
A basic event with no failure rate is a placeholder — mark it as one.
limits: Declared trees with gate-logic validation; probability quantification is out of scope unless declared.

title: Mind map
what: A radial hierarchy: one central topic, branches of subtopics growing outward.
why: Brainstorming needs a shape that rewards adding, not arranging — the map grows the way the conversation does.
when: Workshops, note-taking, scope exploration before any formal structure exists.
read: The centre is the subject; each ring outward is one level more specific.
Sibling order is the order they were declared, not a ranking.
Branches always leave the vertical centre of an entity's left or right side — the root branches from both.
Entities with long note bodies cap at ten rows: a scrollbar pans them, and the lower-right handle resizes the window (presentation only).
pitfalls: Do not force a mind map to hold cross-links — that is a concept map.
More than three levels usually means one branch deserves its own map.
limits: Declared hierarchy rendered radially; no semantics beyond parent/child.

title: Concept map
what: Concepts as nodes linked by labelled, directed propositions — "order contains lines" as a drawn sentence.
why: The linking phrases are the knowledge: two concepts and a verb make a claim a domain expert can confirm or deny.
when: Knowledge elicitation, ontology sketching, curriculum or glossary design.
read: Read node–link–node as a sentence; every arrow carries its linking phrase.
Cycles are allowed and meaningful — unlike a hierarchy.
pitfalls: Do not leave an unlabelled link — a link without a phrase is an assertion of nothing.
Do not draw org-chart habits onto a concept map; cross-links are the point.
limits: Declared propositions rendered as a graph; no logical inference is performed.

title: Organization chart
what: Reporting lines as a tree: units and roles, top down, with names and titles in the boxes.
why: Escalation paths and span-of-control questions are answered by the shape before anyone reads a name.
when: Onboarding docs, reorg proposals, RACI context (who the letters are).
read: Each box is a role or unit; the line above is its manager.
Wide layers are wide spans; deep chains are slow escalations.
pitfalls: Do not draw dotted-line influence as a reporting line — mark it differently or omit it.
A box with two managers is a matrix claim; draw it deliberately.
limits: Declared hierarchy; HR-system accuracy is documented, not synchronised.

title: Work breakdown structure
what: The project as a deliverable tree: each level decomposes its parent into 100% of the work, no more.
why: Estimation and assignment both start from the same tree — the 100% rule is what keeps scope honest.
when: Project initiation, before any schedule network (see the PERT chapter for the dependency view).
read: Each box is a work package or a grouping; children sum to their parent.
The leaves are what gets estimated and assigned — groupings are never "worked".
inputs: The decomposition rule (by outcome, not by department)
pitfalls: Do not decompose by org chart — the WBS is deliverables, not headcount.
A child that overflows its parent's scope breaks the 100% rule.
limits: Declared decomposition; effort and dates belong to the schedule artefacts, not this tree.

title: Family tree / genealogy
what: Three generations: people, partnerships and descent lines in the conventional genealogy layout.
why: Kinship is the oldest diagrammed domain — a good test that the layout handles unions and many-child descent.
when: Genealogies, house/lineage diagrams, any parentage-plus-partnership structure.
read: Boxes are people; horizontal joins are partnerships; vertical drops are descent.
Read one surname line across the generations before reading individuals.
pitfalls: Do not draw descent from one parent when the fact is a partnership's child.
Dates belong in the boxes; the geometry is kinship only.
limits: Declared kinship rendered conventionally; no genealogical validation rules are applied.

title: Icon pack symbols in a network
what: A network drawn with the bundled icon packs: devices and services rendered as recognisable symbols instead of boxes.
why: Ops readers find a router icon faster than a labelled rectangle — recognition beats reading at incident time.
when: Infrastructure diagrams for audiences who know the vendor/icon vocabulary.
read: Icons are declared per element; the node still carries its label and relations.
Count from the catalogue: the icon packs ship with the runtime, nothing loads remotely.
pitfalls: Do not mix metaphors (cloud icon for an on-prem box) to fill space.
An icon does not replace the label — exports and search read the label.
limits: Bundled icon packs only (count from facts.json); custom icons are a publication choice, not assumed.

title: Vendor icon pack (Tabler)
what: The Tabler open icon set applied to a small system map — one of the bundled packs, shown end to end.
why: A neutral, consistent stroke set keeps mixed-vendor diagrams from becoming logo soup.
when: Documentation where vendor-neutral symbols are policy or good taste.
read: Each node declares its Tabler glyph by name; the pack ships in the runtime.
Stroke weight and sizing follow the publication format, not the icon source.
inputs: The glyph names from the pack
pitfalls: Do not hardcode pixel assumptions — the publication format owns sizing.
A missing glyph name fails the render; check diagnostics before blaming layout.
limits: The bundled Tabler subset as declared in the registry; upstream set changes are not tracked live.

title: P&ID symbol library
what: Piping and instrumentation symbols on one sheet: vessels, valves, pumps and instrument bubbles as used in process engineering.
why: P&ID reviews run on symbol recognition; a shared sheet keeps every drawing in the project on the same glyphs.
when: Reference while drawing or reviewing process and instrumentation diagrams.
read: Symbols are grouped by equipment family; each is labelled with its tag role.
Instrument bubbles read by their letter codes, drawn here at working size.
inputs: None — this is a reference sheet
pitfalls: Do not substitute a near-match symbol; P&ID glyphs carry safety meaning.
Keep one symbol scale per drawing.
limits: Common-practice P&ID symbols for documentation; ISA/ISO certification of the set is not claimed.

title: Electrical schematic symbol library
what: Schematic symbols on one sheet: sources, switches, protection and loads as drawn in electrical documentation.
why: Electrical reviews fail on ambiguous glyphs; the sheet fixes the project vocabulary.
when: Reference while drawing or reviewing single-line and schematic diagrams.
read: Symbols are labelled by function; connection points are where wires attach in a real schematic.
Read the sheet alongside the ladder chapter for the logic view of the same domain.
inputs: None — this is a reference sheet
pitfalls: Do not mix IEC and ANSI glyph families on one drawing.
A symbol without terminal points cannot be wired — decoration is not connection.
limits: Common-practice schematic symbols for documentation; standards certification of the set is not claimed.

title: Isometric chart treatment
what: The standard chart marks — bars, pies, areas, treemaps — extruded into an isometric treatment with a declared depth field.
why: Presentations sometimes demand the 3-D look; doing it as a treatment over the same records keeps the data honest.
when: Executive decks and posters, where the audience read the flat chart first.
read: Heights and angles still encode the declared measure; depth is a second declared field, not decoration.
Read values off the flat variants when precision matters — isometric projection distorts by design.
inputs: The measure and the depth field
pitfalls: Do not compare depths across panels — the projection is per-view.
Never let the treatment hide a smaller bar behind a larger one without saying so.
limits: A rendering treatment over declared records; the data contract is identical to the flat charts.

title: Isometric architecture view
what: A platform architecture drawn as an isometric block map: tiers as slabs, systems as blocks on them.
why: The iso view reads like a model of the estate — useful when the audience thinks in buildings, not boxes.
when: Poster architecture overviews and onboarding decks.
read: Slabs are tiers; blocks on a slab are its systems; connectors still carry the declared relations.
The same model renders flat elsewhere — the geometry is a view choice, not data.
pitfalls: Do not let occlusion hide a system — rotate the narrative, not the truth.
Iso is for orientation; detail reviews belong on the flat view.
limits: An isometric projection of the declared model; placement on slabs is declared, not inferred.

title: Geo choropleth
what: Country-level records coloured on a bundled world map — geography as a data view, with the projection named.
why: Distribution questions with a spatial answer deserve a map, and the map ships with the runtime (no remote tiles).
when: Adoption, incident or market data keyed by country code.
read: Colour encodes the declared value per country record; grey is no declared record, not zero.
The map projection (equalEarth here) is declared in the view — area distortion is a choice, not an accident.
pitfalls: Do not key by country name — codes, or the join silently drops rows.
A choropleth normalises nothing; rates versus totals is your modelling decision.
limits: Declared records on the bundled 110m geography; boundary politics follow the asset, not the author.

title: Chen ER notation — extended
what: Classic Chen entity-relationship notation: entity rectangles, relationship diamonds, attribute ovals, extended with the weak/identifying marks.
why: Chen separates the relationship (diamond) from the entity visually — the notation that teaches what a relationship *is*.
when: Teaching, conceptual modelling, or anywhere the relationship itself carries attributes.
read: Rectangles are entities, diamonds are relationships, ovals are attributes; double lines mark total participation.
Cardinality is written as numbers on the connecting lines.
inputs: The relationships (with their own attributes if any)
pitfalls: Do not hang an attribute on a line — it belongs to an entity or a relationship, say which.
A diamond with one entity is usually a missing entity.
limits: Declared ER structure; mapping to a relational schema is the logical-modelling step (see that chapter).

title: Crow's-foot ERD
what: Entities with attribute compartments and crow's-foot cardinality marks at the line ends — the working ERD idiom.
why: The crow's-foot end reads at a glance: one, many, optional — three marks answer most modelling questions.
