when: Logical data modelling sessions where the schema is being agreed in the room.
read: Each box is an entity with its attributes; the end marks read (optionality, cardinality) outward from the entity.
Read a relationship both directions — each end is a separate claim.
pitfalls: Do not mark both ends many without asking where the join entity went.
An attribute everyone updates together is usually an entity in disguise.
limits: Declared ERD with cardinality-mark validation; physical naming and types come later.

title: Cross-file traceability (UAF governance/operations)
what: A strategic-capabilities view whose model is split across files — traces resolve across file boundaries into one render.
why: Real architectures outgrow one file; the trace view proves references stay intact when the model is partitioned.
when: Multi-file models: governance in one file, operations in another, one view over both.
read: The boxes and traces read exactly as a single-file view; the file boundary is invisible in the render.
Imports in the source declare which file supplies which elements.
inputs: The main source file and its included files
pitfalls: External references require the target file and its name, separated by ::.
An included file retains its name scope; loading order never selects a target.
limits: Cross-file references resolved at render time; no external repository or versioning semantics are implied.

title: Drill-down linked views
what: An overview whose elements declare links into a detail view — navigation as part of the model, not the tooling.
why: Reviewers get lost when "see the detail diagram" is a sentence in an email; a declared link is checkable.
when: Any two-level architecture: estate overview plus per-system details.
read: Elements carrying a link are the doorways; the variant is one of the targets.
The overview stays stable while details evolve underneath it.
pitfalls: Do not link to a view that does not exist — diagnostics catch it, reviews should not have to.
Keep the overview to orientation; detail belongs in the target.
limits: Declared links resolved at render/publication time; no hyperlink protocol beyond the documents is implied.

title: External gates with required evidence
what: The governance gates an external party imposes, drawn with the evidence each gate demands before passage.
why: Audit surprises are usually known gates nobody drew; the diagram makes the evidence list a design input.
when: Regulated delivery: planning for audits, certifications, external sign-offs.
read: Gates are the checkpoints; their attached notes list the required evidence.
Read the order — evidence produced out of order is evidence produced twice.
pitfalls: Do not paraphrase a regulator's requirement — quote it and trace your artefact to it.
A gate with no owner produces its evidence at the deadline, badly.
limits: Declared gates and evidence lists; compliance itself is an audit outcome, not a render outcome.

title: Independent verification checklist
what: The software-change review gates with their checklists — independent review drawn as a first-class part of delivery.
why: A checklist that lives in the model gets versioned with it; the one in a wiki page drifts.
when: Change control: releases, schema migrations, anything requiring sign-off.
read: Gates sequence the change; checklist items attach to the gate that enforces them.
Independence is declared — who reviews is part of the model, not a meeting invite.
pitfalls: Do not let the author and reviewer be the same declared role.
A gate that always passes on the nod is theatre — say what evidence it reads.
limits: Declared gates and checklists; enforcement is an organisational act, not a render guarantee.

title: Balanced process contract
what: Interfaces drawn with their declared state and the verification that keeps both sides balanced — the contract as a diagram.
why: Integration defects are contract assumptions colliding; drawing the declared state on each side exposes the mismatch.
when: Interface design between systems or teams, especially asynchronous ones.
read: Each side declares what it provides and expects; the verification marks say how balance is checked.
A state declared on one side with no counterpart is the integration bug you just found early.
pitfalls: Do not leave the verification method as "testing" — name the check.
A balanced contract says nothing about latency; declare that separately.
limits: Declared contracts and verification intent; runtime conformance monitoring is out of scope.

title: Nested fields — domains and representations
what: Fields nested inside elements: domains and physical representations as collapsible rows, with identities that survive the collapse.
why: Logical-to-physical detail belongs on the element, and collapsing must never lose the endpoint a relation lands on.
when: Domain modelling where each attribute carries a type, a domain and a physical representation.
read: Rows inside an element are its nested fields; indentation is the nesting.
The collapsed variant hides rows — relation endpoints still resolve to the same identities.
pitfalls: Do not model a field as a separate box when it belongs to its element.
Collapsing is a view choice — if an endpoint vanishes, that is a defect, not a feature.
limits: Declared nesting with identity preservation validated across collapse; type checking beyond declaration is out of scope.

title: UI wireframe
what: A settings screen as declared regions and controls — layout structure without pixel design.
why: Screen reviews about structure ("what is on this screen, where does this action go") should not need a design tool.
when: Early UI specification, acceptance-criteria discussions, screen-inventory documentation.
read: Nested regions are the layout hierarchy; labelled controls are the interactive elements.
Read tab order off the declaration order, not the visual order.
pitfalls: Do not specify pixels — the wireframe declares structure, the design system owns geometry.
A control with no declared action is a dead end.
limits: Declared structure rendered schematically; no accessibility audit or visual-design conformance is claimed.

title: ETL pipeline — sources to marts
what: A nightly extract-transform-load pipeline in the data-flow idiom: sources, landing, staging, conformance and the marts it feeds.
why: Pipeline reviews fail on invisible handoffs; drawing every read/write makes an unverified hop a visible gap.
when: Batch integration design, data-platform documentation, impact analysis ("who reads this table?").
read: Activities transform; datasets hold; read/write arrows show which direction data moves on each hop.
Trace one field from source to mart — every transform it crosses is a place it can change meaning.
pitfalls: Do not draw a dataset-to-dataset arrow with no activity between — the transform is the point.
A mart nobody declared a consumer for is shelf-ware.
limits: Declared flow in the DFD idiom; job scheduling, data quality and volumes are documented elsewhere.

title: Event contract — producer, schema, consumers
what: One topic with its schema versions, the producing service and the consumer groups — the compatibility claims drawn as a graph.
why: Event breakage is a contract failure; the diagram makes "who may break whom" reviewable before a schema change ships.
when: Event-driven integration: schema registry reviews, deprecation windows, consumer onboarding.
read: The producer publishes to the topic; the topic conforms to the current schema; consumers read in their own groups.
The supersedes edge is the compatibility claim — a consumer on v2 must still read v3 events.
inputs: The schema versions and their compatibility
pitfalls: Do not deprecate a schema version while a declared consumer still reads it.
A consumer group with no declared purpose is an unmanaged dependency.
limits: Declared contract graph; wire-level schema validation against the registry is a runtime concern.

title: Shards and replicas — placement
what: A keyspace split into shards, each shard leading in one failure zone with replicas placed in the others.
why: Placement is a claim you can review: lose one zone and the diagram says which leaders move and which reads degrade.
when: Distributed data design: capacity planning, failure-mode review, migration planning.
read: Shards are key ranges; "leads in" edges name the primary zone, "replica" edges the copies.
Count copies per zone — two shards leading in the same zone concentrates failover risk.
inputs: The shards and their key ranges
pitfalls: Do not place all of a shard's copies in one zone — that is a backup, not replication.
The router must know every shard; a range gap loses writes.
limits: Declared placement; consensus, failover timing and consistency levels are design decisions documented elsewhere.

title: Subdiagrams and inline views
what: A view that links to another view, and an embedded view that keeps its own composition inside the host diagram.
why: Detail-on-demand without leaving the page: the overview stays readable while the detail is one declared hop away.
when: Layered documentation: estate overviews with per-area details, poster diagrams with magnified insets.
read: Linked elements open their target view; the inline variant draws the embedded view's own layout inside the host.
The embedded view keeps its composition — moving the host does not rearrange it.
pitfalls: Do not nest inline views more than the composition rules allow — one level deep, by rule.
A link target that does not exist fails validation, not silently.
limits: Declared links and embedding with composition validation; no interactive navigation is shipped in the static SVG.

title: Roadmap timeline — phases on one axis
what: A programme roadmap: phases as bars on one time axis, the gating dependencies between them declared.
why: A roadmap is the schedule at phase granularity — sequence and overlap are the argument, task tracking lives elsewhere.
when: Programme communication: steering packs, planning baselines, dependency-aware phasing.
read: Each bar is a phase with declared start and end dates; arrows are the finish-to-start gates.
Overlap between bars is a declared choice — find the gate that still holds across it.
pitfalls: Do not track tasks on the roadmap — one bar per phase, or it stops being one.
A phase with no gate in or out is either the boundary of the programme or a missing dependency.
limits: Declared dates and dependencies (finish-to-start validated); capacity and criticality analysis belong to the PERT chapter.

title: Looks — classic, hand-drawn and neo
what: The same model rendered in each built-in look: precise single strokes, organic pen strokes, raised precise cards.
why: The look is a view choice, not data — the right reading context (review vs workshop vs deck) picks the look.
when: Choosing a house style, or matching the diagram to the meeting: hand-drawn invites change, classic asserts precision.
read: Switch variants: the model, layout and labels are identical — only the stroke treatment changes.
Hand-drawn is deterministic here, not random: the same source always renders the same strokes.
inputs: The look declaration on the view
pitfalls: Do not signal "draft" with a hand-drawn look on a baselined model — say the status in words.
Never compare measurements across looks; strokes differ, data does not.
limits: The three built-in looks; custom strokes are a publication-format concern, not assumed here.

title: Route options — curved, orthogonal and rounded
what: Relation routing as a declaration: curved flows, orthogonal corridors, rounded corners — and per-relation overrides.
why: Routing is readability infrastructure: the same graph reads cleanly or not at all depending on the corridors.
when: Dense diagrams, publication-quality output, or matching a house routing style.
read: Switch variants: same graph, different route geometry — curved for organic flow, orthogonal for engineering reading.
The mixed variant shows overrides: one view, independent route styles per relation.
inputs: The routing declaration per view or per relation
pitfalls: Do not mix route styles without a reason — the mixed variant is a capability demo, not a recommendation.
A route is never a fact: crossings and curves carry no semantics.
limits: Declared routing options; the router optimises within the declaration, it does not infer intent.

title: Crossings — gaps, bridges and square jumps
what: How disconnected lines cross: a gap, a rounded jump, or a local square jump — the mark that says "not connected".
why: A crossing misread as a junction is a defect that ships; the crossing mark is the honest "no connection here".
when: Any routed diagram where unrelated lines must cross — bus layouts, networks, wiring.
read: Find the crossing: the mark (gap, bridge or square) belongs to the line that hops, and it means exactly one thing.
Connected lines join at a node; crossed lines pass — the mark removes the ambiguity.
The router minimizes crossings first (optimize: crossings is the default and keeps improving); the mark disambiguates the crossings that remain, it does not excuse a tangled layout.
pitfalls: Do not rely on colour alone to separate crossing lines — marks survive print and colour-blindness.
One crossing style per diagram; mixed marks reintroduce the ambiguity.
limits: Crossing marks are presentation disambiguation; connectivity is declared in the model, never inferred from geometry.

title: Keyed record fields and compact declarations
what: Records addressed by stable keys (refresh-safe), and the one-line view-header form that expands to a canonical declaration.
why: Keys make data refreshes order-independent; the compact header makes small views writable without boilerplate.
when: Data-bound views that refresh, and any view small enough to say in one line.
read: The chart binds records by key — reordered or refreshed data lands on the same bars.
The variant shows the compact form: one header line desugars to the same data + projection the verbose form declares.
inputs: The compact header form for small views
pitfalls: Do not rely on record order once keys exist — keys are the contract.
The compact form expands to canonical declarations; if you need more, write the verbose form.
limits: Keyed binding and header desugaring as specified; no schema inference beyond the declared records.

title: Layout algorithms — picking the placement
what: One small hierarchy rendered by each native placement algorithm: grid, layered, tree, circular, radial, organic and more.
why: The algorithm is the argument structure: layered reads as flow, tree as descent, radial as containment — pick deliberately.
when: Any new view: choose the placement that matches the question before tuning anything else.
read: Switch variants: same six elements, same relations — only the placement changes.
Read the layered variant for direction, the radial for orbit distance, the grid for census.
inputs: The algorithm declaration (and its root/columns/direction where relevant)
pitfalls: Do not hand-tune positions before the algorithm is right — that is fighting the tool.
A tree algorithm on a cyclic graph hides the cycles; check the relation kinds first.
limits: The registry's native and pattern algorithms; custom placement is the pinned-placement technique.

title: Spacing hints — tight to expanded
what: The same diagram at four declared spacings: tight, normal, loose, expanded.
why: Density is a reading-speed choice: tight for overview posters, expanded for step-by-step walkthroughs.
when: Fitting a diagram to its medium — slide, A4 page, or wall chart.
read: Switch variants: nothing moves semantically; the corridors widen or narrow.
Text size does not shrink with spacing — below the minimum the publication rule complains.
pitfalls: Do not fix crowding with spacing when the real problem is too many elements per view.
Tight spacing plus long labels is a collision you declared.
limits: Declared spacing hints within the engine's minimum clearances; it will not overlap elements to satisfy a hint.

title: Publication — page size, fit and minimum text
what: The same semantic model published two ways: an A4 page with explicit minimum text size, and a content-sized screen render.
why: The publication block is the contract with the reader's medium — the engine warns instead of shipping unreadable text.
when: Anything leaving the screen: print packs, PDF reports, ISO-style documentation sets.
read: The paper variant fits the model to A4 and declares the smallest text allowed; the screen variant sizes to content.
Overflow is a diagnostic, not a silent crop — read the warnings before exporting.

Headers, footers, borders and backgrounds live in the same publication block (see the Publication chrome chapter), and --content-size forces the content-sized form for one render without editing the source.
inputs: The publication declaration (size, fit, orientation, minimum text)
pitfalls: Do not raise the scale by shrinking text below the declared minimum — split the view instead.
A fit: none choice means you own the extents; check the page in the export, not the preview.
limits: Declared publication rules with overflow/minimum-text diagnostics; print-driver behaviour is outside the model.

title: Authorized export — hiding is not redaction
what: A private source view next to its allowlisted public export: the public view shows exactly what the allowlist names.
why: Hidden elements still ship in the SVG source unless the export excludes them — hiding is not redaction, exclusion is.
when: External publication of internal models: customer-facing diagrams, tenders, regulatory submissions.
read: The private view shows everything; the public variant renders only the allowlisted elements and relations.
Anything not on the allowlist is absent from the export artefact — check the variant, then the export.
pitfalls: Do not publish the private SVG because "it looks clean" — inspect the allowlisted export instead.
Labels on allowlisted elements can still leak: review wording, not just membership.
limits: Allowlist-based exclusion at render/export time; legal review of what may be published remains a human act.

title: Notation atlas — the semantic silhouettes
what: The composable semantic silhouettes on one sheet: the shapes the notation assigns to meaning, drawn as a reference atlas.
why: Reading any DDN diagram starts with shape recognition — the atlas is the one-page key to all of them.
when: Onboarding to the notation, or checking which silhouette a kind will draw before you use it.
read: Each cell is one silhouette with its name; shapes compose (border, fill, glyph) from the kind's declaration.
Find the shape from a diagram you are reading, then read its meaning here.
inputs: None — this is a reference sheet generated from the registry
pitfalls: Do not memorise colour — colour is theme, silhouette is meaning.
A shape you cannot find here is a custom publication choice, not registry notation.
limits: The installed registry's silhouettes; kind counts always trace to facts.json, never to this page's prose.

title: Pinned placement — anchors in an automatic layout
what: Automatic placement with declared anchors: the pinned elements hold their positions, the algorithm places everything else around them.
why: Real diagrams have landmarks ("the customer is always top-left"); pins say which positions are intentional and which are computed.
when: Any layout where some positions carry meaning — geography, org convention, reader habit.
read: The pinned elements are the fixed points; every other position derives from the algorithm working around them.
Switch variants to see the same pins honoured by different algorithms.
inputs: The algorithm that works around them
pitfalls: Do not pin everything — that is the manual algorithm wearing a costume.
A pin that contradicts the reading order fights the reader, not the engine.
limits: Declared pins honoured by the placement engine; pixel-perfect composition belongs to the manual algorithm.

title: Paused placement — retaining the current scene
what: Auto-placement switched off for a view: the engine retains the current positions and refuses to re-derive them.
why: A reviewed layout is a reviewed artefact — pausing freezes what was approved while the model keeps evolving underneath.
when: Baselined publication views, and any diagram whose composition was agreed in a review.
read: The scene renders retained positions; new elements still need a declared seed position.
The info diagnostic (auto-placement paused) is the engine stating the contract, not an error.
pitfalls: Do not pause early — pausing freezes today's accidents along with today's decisions.
A new element with no seed position under paused placement is a declaration gap you must fill.
limits: Retention of declared/current positions with auto_place off; it preserves positions, not model semantics.

title: Night and low-light palettes
what: The same sheet rendered in the night and dark themes across looks — palettes built for projection and low-light rooms.
why: A diagram projected in a dark room inverts its reading: the night palette keeps contrast where the eye expects it.
when: Ops-room displays, evening reviews, any projected reading in low light.
read: Switch variants: the model is identical; ink, surface and accent move to the night scale.
Contrast pairs stay deliberate — night is a designed palette, not an inverted filter.
inputs: The theme declaration on the view
pitfalls: Do not screenshot a day palette into a night deck — declare the theme and re-render.
Theme is view-level; a mixed-theme document is a deliberate choice, say so.
limits: The built-in theme scales (default, neutral, dark, night, forest, base); custom palettes are a publication-format concern.

title: Data refresh — swapping records without breaking the view
what: A chart whose data block is swapped wholesale — new records, same keys, same bindings — plus the dependency graph reading of the same model.
why: Refreshes are the normal case, not the exception: a view that breaks on new data was wired to the data, not the contract.
when: Operational dashboards, periodic re-publication, any view fed by a changing extract.
read: The chart re-renders from the swapped records; bindings follow keys, not positions.
The variant shows the model behind the refresh — the dependency graph does not change when only values do.
inputs: The data block with stable keys
pitfalls: Do not change the key space in a refresh without migrating the bindings.
A refresh that changes shape (fields, not values) is a schema change — version it.
limits: Record-swap refresh through the declared block; streaming or incremental updates are a host concern.

title: Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram
what: Ishikawa cause-and-effect: one stated effect at the head, possible causes grouped along the bones by category.
why: Investigations stall when causes are a list; the bones force grouping, and grouping exposes the empty category.
when: Problem analysis: incidents, defects, audit findings — before any corrective action is chosen.
read: The head is the effect being explained; each bone is a declared cause category, ribs are the candidate causes.
An empty bone is a finding ("we have no hypothesis here"), not a drawing error.
pitfalls: Do not draw corrective actions as causes — the diagram explains, it does not prescribe.
A cause placed on the wrong bone misdirects the investigation; the category is part of the claim.
limits: Declared causes with fishbone layout validation; root-cause truth is established by the investigation, not the diagram.

title: Whiteboard wall — sticky notes and string
what: The collaborative workshop idiom: free-form sticky notes in six paper colours, push-pins and tape, with sagging string relations between the notes they connect.
why: Early workshops die in record-keeping tooling; a sticky note carries one thought and no structure, so the wall stays at the speed of the conversation.
when: Discovery workshops, brainstorming, affinity grouping, retrospectives — anywhere the model is not yet agreed.
read: Each note is its body text only — no name header, no fields, no kind chip; the colour is a declared x_sticky choice.
A string relation sags like pinned thread: it says "these two belong together" and nothing more.
pitfalls: Do not put fields on a sticky note — the moment a note has rows it is an entity and should be modelled as one.
String is presentation routing: it carries the relation, never adds meaning to it.
limits: Six declared paper colours and the pin/tape decorations; free placement on an infinite canvas is a host-tool concern, the wall uses declared layout.

title: Presentation diagrams — illustration art with connection points
what: The slide-deck idiom: detailed illustrations (people, buildings, servers, vehicles) instead of stroke icons, with relations glued to the artwork’s declared connection anchors.
why: Stakeholder communication reads pictures faster than notation; an art pack gives the deck idiom without giving up a real model underneath.
when: Executive overviews, sales and training material, any audience that should see a factory, not a rect labelled factory.
read: Separate the semantic role from its optional illustration.
Connections still bind declared definitions and members.
Review missing-asset diagnostics instead of treating a placeholder as the intended illustration.
inputs: A registered art pack (CLI --pack or registerArtPack)
pitfalls: Art is presentation: without the pack registered, every node draws an honest placeholder — never fake the artwork inline.
Do not put fields on art nodes; the illustration owns the body area.
limits: Host-registered packs only (never inlined into the tools); 64 KiB per item; anchors are the four side midpoints in the shipped pack.

title: Source versions — the fixed language and default contract
what: A DDN file binds its language and standard defaults to ddn-next-1. Omitting the version selects that same fixed contract, not the newest software defaults.
why: A document must keep its meaning and defaults when the software changes.
when: Creating a file, combining included files, or reviewing a future language revision.
read: Use version ddn-next-1 at file level when an explicit header is useful.
Included files must use the same supported language/default contract.
Changing standard defaults requires a new contract version.
inputs: The source file and its included files
pitfalls: The deprecated prototype grammar is not a second supported mode.
Do not interpret a missing version as permission to select arbitrary new defaults.
limits: Unsupported versions are diagnosed explicitly; this example is converted to the new dialect.

title: View profiles — choosing symbols and rules
what: A view selects a profile that defines its method, projection, palette, legal relationships and verification rules.
why: A declared kind turns "this looks wrong" into a coded diagnostic: permissive mode reports each out-of-vocabulary element as DDN-VP03, strict mode fails the check with DDN-VP04 naming the fix.
when: Any view that claims to follow a notation: declare the kind, then choose strict for regulated deliverables and permissive while drafting.
read: An explicit view declaration uses as followed by its registered profile identifier.
Native short forms supply a particular recipe; they do not merge rules from different methods.
Lifecycle status is separate from profile and drawing style.
inputs: The definitions and data the view presents
pitfalls: Do not select a profile only because its symbols look similar.
A draft status permits incomplete design but does not turn illegal references into resolved ones.
limits: Profiles have bounded contracts. Their presence does not imply a complete execution engine for the external method.

variants.title: Permissive variant with a guest note

title: Numbered technical figures — references and monochrome output
what: A technical figure can use numbered labels, cross-references and restrained presentation to support a larger document.
why: Legal figures live by their numerals: the specification text references "valve 106", and a numeral that drifts from its element invalidates the page. Anchors computed at render time cannot drift.
when: Patent drawings, legal exhibits and any filing that must survive black-and-white reproduction with numbered parts.
read: Read a figure number or reference together with its referenced content.
Use redundant shape, text and line distinctions when preparing monochrome output.
Check the final output size and text legibility.
pitfalls: A diagramming tool does not establish legal filing compliance.
A displayed reference must resolve to the intended item, not merely have a plausible label.
limits: This is a technical documentation example. Legal compliance and filing acceptance are outside the diagram contract.

title: Publication — page furniture and composed output
what: A document view organizes model content for a target output, with page size, captions, headers, footers and other declared presentation settings.
why: Titles, dates, page numbers and figure numbers belong in the source, not in a post-processing step — one declaration keeps every exported page consistent and reviewable.
when: Print packs, release documentation, filings — anything that leaves the screen as a set of numbered pages.
read: Distinguish the content bounds from the document page and its margins.
Inspect captions, references and page furniture at the final output size.
Check the exporter capabilities installed in the utility before selecting an output format.
pitfalls: An output-format declaration does not install an exporter.
A snapshot does not automatically remain live after export.
limits: The document contract and installed export capabilities are separate; unsupported formats must be reported explicitly.

title: Text fit — wrapping, bounds and visible overflow
what: Text layout balances readable type with available geometry. Table cells wrap on screen while each data row remains one physical source line.
why: Hand-tuning box sizes against text that keeps changing is the chore text_fit removes — with bounds and diagnostics so adaptation stays honest instead of silently clipping.
when: Long labels, generated text, multilingual content — anywhere text length is not under the author's full control.
read: Inspect the complete label and the space available to it.
Table columns may specify minimum width in default-font characters and maximum wrapped lines.
Ellipsis marks clipped text; an unfit table uses the shaded-square indicator.
pitfalls: Do not use physical multiline source rows to force table wrapping.
A readable preview at one zoom does not establish legibility in a smaller exported page.
limits: Text measurement and target output affect geometry. Semantic identity and relationships remain distinct from wrapping.

title: Text presentation — readable typography and Markdown
what: Use registered font and text properties for overall presentation, and supported Markdown inside narrative text for local emphasis.
why: Emphasis that lives only in a viewer's session preview vanishes on export; declared in the model it survives publication, diffing and hand-off to any conformant tool.
when: A label that must read as retired (strike), a display name in small caps, an emphasised (bold/italic) element, a coloured label, or decorated header/footer chrome.
read: File settings override eligible CSS presentation settings, then standard defaults apply.
Notes support headings, emphasis, strong emphasis, lists and the DDN underline extension.
Identifiers and typed data remain plain unless their role explicitly supports formatting.
inputs: The intended font and supported formatting
pitfalls: Raw HTML is not interpreted as arbitrary page content.
Do not change an identifier just to obtain a different displayed title.
limits: Formatting follows the supported DDN text profile and the selected role’s property contract.

title: Connector presentation — color, weight and pattern
what: Registered line and stroke properties change presentation while a connection retains its semantic role and endpoints.
why: Emphasis that lives in a viewer's session-preview CSS vanishes on export; declared in the model, a thicker dashed boundary or a coloured flow survives publication and hand-off.
when: A de-emphasised or highlighted flow (dotted, coloured), a heavier element boundary, a tinted card fill — paint distinctions that are not registry semantics.
read: Read the relation role and endpoint markers before relying on color.
View and occurrence settings can change presentation within their property contract.
Routing geometry and semantic endpoint selection are distinct from stroke styling.
pitfalls: Color alone is an unreliable semantic distinction.
A heavier or dashed line must not silently change the relation type.
limits: Use only the applicable codex properties; the profile still controls legal connections.

title: Sizing and opacity — scoped presentation overrides
what: Individual appearances can override eligible presentation values without replacing the underlying shared definition.
why: A local display adjustment should have an explicit scope and preserve the model’s identity.
when: A single oversized note in an otherwise uniform diagram, a draft node that should recede visually, a tight caption with its own shrink floor.
read: Check whether a setting belongs to the shared definition, one occurrence or the view.
Omitted property leaves continue through the declared default hierarchy.
Opacity changes appearance; it does not remove data from the model.
pitfalls: Making an item invisible is not redaction.
Do not copy a shared definition merely to change one appearance.
limits: Each property follows the codex ownership and default rules; output measurement remains a separate concern.

title: Reusable templates — shared structure and explicit parameters
what: Reusable definitions and registered templates reduce repetition while retaining explicit identity and source ownership.
why: A pipeline of identical stages is one template, not five copies to keep in sync: rename the stage kind or add a field once and every instance follows — with identities exactly as if you had typed each stage out.
when: Repeated sub-models (stages, tiers, mirrored pairs), template libraries shared across files, any place a copy-paste block keeps drifting.
read: Inspect the template or shared definition before changing one of its uses.
A template expansion is derived content; edit the defining source or the permitted instance settings.
References preserve identity independently of displayed labels.
pitfalls: Do not assume prototype fragment punctuation remains valid in the new dialect.
Avoid accidental duplicate declarations when an appearance can reuse existing content.
limits: Only the adopted template and reference rules apply; parsing declarations does not execute arbitrary programs.

title: Comparing views — identity before appearance
what: A before-and-after comparison is useful when definitions keep stable identity and the compared scopes are explicit.
why: Reviewing a change means seeing it, not reconstructing it from two files: one picture shows what appeared, what vanished and what moved — generated from the model, never hand-drawn.
when: Migration plans, review packets, change proposals, before/after teaching material — anywhere two revisions of a model need one shared reading.
read: Separate added, removed and changed definitions from presentation-only changes.
A title change need not change identity.
Connections have their own content and must be checked independently of endpoint appearance.
inputs: The two identified revisions or model scopes
pitfalls: Similar labels do not prove that two definitions are the same item.
A visible before-and-after layout is not by itself evidence of a computed semantic diff.
limits: The converted example preserves the supplied comparison material. Inspect the current view’s declared data and available analysis rather than assuming prototype diff syntax.

title: Markings and metadata — claims with explicit meaning
what: Annotations, status and provenance carry distinct design claims. They must be read with their property and profile contracts.
why: "This path must not exist" and "this box is a draft" are design facts; keeping them in the model means they export, diff and render under every theme — instead of living in someone's slide notes.
when: Migration plans (forbidden legacy paths), drafts under review (tentative scope), machine-generated documents (generator provenance), and audit claims (assertions).
read: Separate lifecycle status from drawing style and from other semantic annotations.
An assertion needs evidence when its contract requires evidence.
A successful render does not make a claim true or accept the design.
inputs: Its owner and applicable metadata contract
pitfalls: A visual marker alone is not an authorization or acceptance record.
Do not use annotations to erase an inconvenient dependency.
limits: Verification checks declared contracts and supplied information; it cannot establish facts about an unobserved external system.

title: Programmatic verification — scopes and diagnostic results
what: The independent verifier and shared runtime allow a host to inspect source, references and profile rules without granting editing through a viewer.
why: Scripts and CI need answers, not pictures: which verb may connect these kinds, which diagnostics fired and where, and whether the page survives print rules — all without opening a tool.
when: Authoring assistance (verbs), CI gates (--diagnostics json, --strict-print), documentation pipelines (publish) and quick previews (--content-size).
read: Choose the verification scope and supply the complete source set.
Inspect diagnostics, completeness and unsupported capabilities explicitly.
Keep loading, verification, editing and exporting as distinct host responsibilities.
inputs: The entry file and included source files
The requested scope and completion level
pitfalls: The deprecated prototype CLI commands are not the new utility API.
A successful source parse alone does not establish semantic completeness.
limits: Use the current module APIs. Automated deployment, arbitrary code execution and external process enforcement are outside this example.

title: Whiteboard / discovery sketch
what: A preliminary map of named concepts and their relationships. An unspecified object deliberately leaves storage technology and detailed structure undecided; it is not an undocumented SQL table.
why: Use this to expose disagreements about vocabulary before implementation choices obscure them. A shared sketch provides stable identities that can acquire fields, domains and deployment details later.
when: Start an unfamiliar project or facilitate a meeting where participants need to agree on the important things before they agree on keys and types.
read: Read the nouns in the boxes first.
Read each connecting verb as an assertion, not as an enforced foreign key.
An unselected element is out of scope for this sketch, not deleted from the model.
inputs: Questions that have not been settled
pitfalls: Do not infer a table from every rectangle.
Do not treat proximity, colour, or a crossed line as a new fact.
limits: This is an explanatory model, not an executed business system. A successful render does not establish implementation effectiveness or independent approval.

title: Conceptual business ER diagram
what: Entities and the relationships between them at business level: names and cardinalities, no storage design.
why: Agree on the things the business tracks before any schema discussion; the diagram is the vocabulary contract.
when: Early domain workshops and any review where business stakeholders must confirm scope without reading SQL.
read: Entities are nouns; relationships are verbs with cardinality marks.
Participation marks (zero/one/many) are claims about the domain, not constraints enforced here.
inputs: How they relate, in business words
pitfalls: Do not start assigning datatypes here — that is the logical/physical stage.
A relationship without a business-readable verb is usually a missing entity.
limits: Conceptual only: no keys, types or indexes are decided by this view.

title: BPMN collaboration / message flow between pools
what: Two pools with their internal flows and the message flow between them: the classic BPMN collaboration picture.
why: Make cross-organisation communication explicit without pretending one party controls the other.
when: Whenever a process crosses an organisational boundary and responsibilities must stay visibly separate.
read: Each pool owns its sequence flow; message flow only connects across pools.
A message flow inside one pool is a modeling error, not a style choice.
pitfalls: Do not draw sequence flow between pools.
Do not hide a participant whose messages drive your process.
limits: Notation coverage only: no execution, simulation or choreography conformance is claimed by this render.

title: Bar chart — live records, keyed refresh
what: A data-bound bar chart over a records block: the records are the source, the chart is a projection of them.
why: Show that the chart is generated from data you can replace — the supported live-dashboard pattern is a transactional record swap, not an image swap.
when: Any metric over categories where the numbers will change but the model must not.
read: Bars read value against unit by category.
The source data block is one summary away in the Files panel.
inputs: A data block to own them
pitfalls: Do not edit the picture when the data is wrong — edit the records.
Do not reorder keyed records expecting identities to follow position.
limits: Bounded native marks and finite JavaScript arithmetic; refresh replaces records, never structure.

title: IEC 61131-3 ladder diagram / relay logic
what: Three rungs between the power rails: normally-open and normally-closed contacts driving coils, one coil per rung, a parallel OR branch, and a hosted function block.
why: Ladder logic is the control-room reading of combinatorial logic: conditions left-to-right, one output per rung.
when: Industrial control documentation where electricians and engineers share one reading of the wiring.
read: Power flows conceptually left rail to right rail.
Contacts in series are AND; contacts stacked on parallel tracks are OR.
One rung drives exactly one coil — the validator enforces it.
pitfalls: A rung with two coils is an error, not a design.
Branches come from the wiring topology — you do not declare them.
limits: Common-practice ladder rendering and validation; no PLC compilation, execution or IEC XML interchange.

title: Typed decision table — first match
what: A typed decision table evaluated in first-match order: the first row whose conditions all match produces the outcome.
why: Expose rule order as a deliberate design decision instead of an accident of presentation.
when: Bounded business rules where precedence must be reviewable line by line.
read: Read rows top-down: the first fully-matching row wins.
Type domains on each input gate what a row may claim.
inputs: The input fields and their domains
The rule rows in priority order
pitfalls: Row order is normative here — reordering rows changes outcomes.
A gap in the domain is a silent fall-through, not a default row.
limits: Bounded decision-table evaluation against one input record; no arbitrary rule-language execution.
